content: When a query filters a large orders table by one customer and a short date interval, what determines whether the database scans the table or uses an index?

The optimizer compares estimated costs. It considers available indexes, predicate selectivity, table size, data distribution, and the cost of fetching matching rows. An index on customer and date can identify a narrow region efficiently, but a table scan may still win if the filter matches much of the table or if many scattered row lookups would be expensive. Statistics drive that estimate.

How does a B-tree handle the two predicate types differently? Equality seems like finding one position, while a date interval might require visiting many neighboring keys and then retrieving several rows.

For equality, traversal descends through ordered internal pages to the leaf range containing the target value. For a range, the tree similarly finds the first boundary, then walks linked leaf pages until it passes the other boundary. Either operation may produce many row references. The initial location is efficient; total work still grows with the number of matching index entries and required table fetches.

I might be wrong, but I think a B-tree index accelerates selective equality and range filters by locating relevant keys without scanning every table row...? Would low selectivity explain why the optimizer sometimes ignores it?

Yes, that is the central benefit, and selectivity explains the apparent exception. The tree narrows access to relevant keys, but each match can still require visibility checks or a base-table lookup. When a predicate returns a large fraction of rows, those scattered operations may cost more than reading the table sequentially. An optimizer can therefore choose a scan even though the index is usable.
What should I inspect in an execution plan to confirm that distinction? I want to tell apart the cost of reaching the first matching key from the cost of processing all returned rows.

Look for the access node, its index condition, estimated versus actual rows, loops, and timing when your database reports it. An index seek or range scan shows how candidates are located; a following table lookup shows extra retrieval work. Compare startup time with total time, and note rows removed by residual filters. Buffer or page-read statistics can reveal whether random fetches dominate.
If two tables contain the same number of rows, can their B-tree equality lookups take noticeably different time because of tree height, cache state, or duplicate values?

They can. Tree height depends on key width, page size, fill level, and fan-out, not just row count. Cached upper and leaf pages avoid storage reads, while a cold lookup may wait for I/O. Duplicate values also change the amount of leaf scanning and row retrieval after the first match. Concurrency, visibility checks, and fragmented storage can widen the difference further.
Is the usual logarithmic description only about descending the tree? I am trying to separate the comparison count used to locate a boundary from the work required to return all qualifying records.

Primarily, yes. Searching a balanced B-tree takes work proportional to its height, commonly summarized as logarithmic in the number of indexed entries. After reaching the boundary, the engine must scan matching leaf entries and possibly fetch rows, giving a rough cost of O(log n + m), where m is the result count. Hardware pages and caching matter more in practice than literal comparison counts.

I might be wrong, but I think a B-tree index guarantees constant-time equality and range filters by locating every relevant key with a single comparison...? Does the high branching factor make that effectively true?

A high branching factor makes the tree shallow, but it does not provide that guarantee. The engine generally visits several levels to reach a leaf, and a range or nonunique equality match can span many leaf entries. In asymptotic terms, locating the start is logarithmic and returning m matches adds work proportional to m. A warm cache may make a few page visits feel nearly constant at ordinary sizes.
How would a hash index change this analysis for equality predicates, and why would it still be unsuitable for a query asking for values between two ordered bounds?

A hash index uses a hash-derived bucket, so equality lookup has expected constant-time behavior under favorable load and collision assumptions, though it is not an unconditional one-comparison guarantee. Hashing discards key order: nearby values need not occupy nearby buckets. Consequently, an interval has no contiguous region to traverse, whereas a B-tree stores keys in order and can walk successive leaves.
Why can adding several useful-looking indexes make an insert-heavy workload slower even when none of the new indexes is referenced by the application’s read queries yet?

Every inserted row must also be represented in each applicable index. The database finds the proper leaf page, writes an entry, records recovery information, and may split or rebalance pages. More indexes therefore mean more CPU, memory pressure, logging, and storage I/O. Constraints backed by indexes add validation work too. Whether reads currently use those structures does not remove their maintenance cost.
Do updates always touch every index, or only indexes involving changed columns? I am also wondering whether row relocation can create maintenance work even when an indexed value remains identical.

The exact behavior is engine-specific. An update normally requires logical index changes when an indexed key or included column changes. Some storage designs can avoid rewriting unaffected index entries; others must update row locators when the base row moves. MVCC may create new row versions and leave cleanup for later. Thus unchanged keys often reduce work, but they do not universally make index maintenance disappear.

I might be wrong, but I think indexes speed many reads but add storage and write overhead because inserts, updates, and deletes also modify index structures...? Is that the main tradeoff when choosing them?

That is the main tradeoff. An index offers an additional access path for reads, but its pages consume space and must remain transactionally consistent with the table. Inserts and deletes add or retire entries, while relevant updates may change them. Selection should therefore reflect actual query value, write rate, key width, redundancy with existing indexes, and maintenance effects such as vacuuming or page splits.
What measurements would help decide whether one index earns its cost? Query latency is obvious, but I would also like to capture write amplification, cache pressure, and maintenance burden.

Compare representative workloads before and after the index, not isolated queries alone. Record read-plan changes, latency distributions, rows and pages examined, transaction throughput, log volume, storage growth, and buffer-cache hit rates. Track page splits, dead entries, vacuum or compaction time, and index usage counters where available. Allow statistics and caches to stabilize, then evaluate peak write periods as well as average traffic.
During an UPDATE that changes a customer’s email address, which database structures participate besides the heap or clustered table, and how does the transaction keep them mutually consistent?

The engine may update every index containing the email as a key or included value, plus constraint indexes and recovery logs. Under MVCC it may create a new row version rather than overwrite in place. Locks, latches, or versioning protect concurrent access, while the transaction log makes the table and index changes recoverable as one atomic unit. Precise steps vary by storage engine.
If an index does not include the email column, can that update still affect it? I am thinking about indexes whose leaf entries store a physical locator or primary key for the changed row.

Possibly. If the row stays at the same locator and the index contains no changed data, an engine may leave that index untouched. If updating creates a new physical version or changes the clustered key used as the locator, secondary entries may need adjustment or later cleanup. Some engines preserve stable tuple identifiers; others use primary-key values. The storage model determines the indirect cost.

I might be wrong, but I think indexes speed many reads without affecting writes because inserts, updates, and deletes modify only the underlying table rows...? Could index maintenance happen later without delaying the transaction?

Ordinary indexes must reflect committed changes, so writes generally do affect them. An insert adds entries, a delete removes or marks them obsolete, and relevant updates replace them; the transaction usually performs or logs that work before commit. Some cleanup, compaction, or index building can be deferred, but deferring all logical maintenance would let subsequent queries return missing or stale results. Specialized asynchronous indexes have different consistency guarantees.
How do deferred cleanup and immediate logical maintenance differ under MVCC? A deleted row may remain physically present, so I want to understand what an index scan is allowed to encounter.

Immediate logical maintenance ensures the index and transaction metadata lead readers to the correct visible version under their snapshot. A scan may still encounter an entry pointing to a dead or invisible row and reject it during a visibility check. Deferred cleanup later reclaims those obsolete entries and row versions safely, once no active snapshot needs them. This separation preserves correctness while moving physical reclamation off the critical path.
For an index defined on country, city, and created_at, which WHERE clauses can use its ordering directly, and where does the leftmost-prefix idea stop being useful?

The ordering is primarily by country, then city within each country, then created_at within each country-city pair. Predicates fixing country can seek into a contiguous region; adding city narrows it further, and adding created_at can define a smaller range. Without a country condition, rows for one city are scattered among country groups, though some engines can use skip scans or scan the whole index.
Suppose the query filters country exactly and uses a range on city. Can created_at also narrow the seek, or does the first range predicate prevent later columns from defining one contiguous interval?

Usually the city range ends the fully contiguous seek prefix. For each country, many city values in that range contain their own created_at sequences, so one condition on created_at does not describe a single narrower interval across all of them. The engine may apply created_at as an index-level residual filter, use multiple seeks, or exploit newer skip-scan techniques, but it typically cannot extend the basic seek boundary directly.
I might be wrong, but I think a composite B-tree index on columns A and B supports filtering by A because A is its leading column...? Would selecting only A also allow an index-only scan?

Yes. Entries are grouped first by A, so an equality or range condition on A identifies a contiguous part of the index even without constraining B. Selecting only A may permit an index-only scan because the requested value is present, but the engine may still consult the base table for visibility information or other metadata. Whether that extra lookup is avoidable depends on the database and page state.
How should ORDER BY influence the same index choice? For example, when A is fixed, can rows be returned in B order without a separate sort, including for descending output?

With A fixed to one value, the matching index region is ordered by B, so the engine can often satisfy ORDER BY B through an ordered scan. Many B-trees can scan backward for descending output. Mixed directions across several sort columns depend on how the index directions were defined and what the engine supports. Null ordering, collation, and expressions must also match the requested ordering.
A query filters by status but the available index is on tenant_id followed by status. Why might the optimizer scan that index instead of seeking directly to the requested status value?

Because status values are not globally contiguous in that ordering. The index contains each tenant's status groups separately, so a single status appears in many regions. The optimizer might still scan a narrower index instead of a wide table, apply a status filter to its entries, or perform a skip scan across tenant values. None of those is the same as one direct seek to a global status range.
Would knowing that tenant_id has only five distinct values change the plan? Repeating a small number of seeks sounds different from scanning millions of index entries.

Yes. With only five tenant values, the engine can conceptually perform five seeks, one into each tenant's status region, and combine the results. Some optimizers implement this as skip scanning or generate comparable plans from statistics. Its attractiveness depends on distinct-count estimates, requested status selectivity, caching, and row-fetch cost. With thousands of tenant values, repeated seeks may cease to be competitive.
I might be wrong, but I think a composite B-tree index on columns A and B supports filtering by B equally well because column order is irrelevant...? Do skip scans make the two orders equivalent?

Column order is significant. An index on (A, B) groups B values separately inside every A group, so filtering on B alone usually lacks one contiguous seek range. A skip scan can reduce the penalty when A has few distinct values, but it performs repeated work and is not universally supported. If B-only filtering is important and selective, an index beginning with B is generally the more direct access path.
When both columns are constrained by equality, does reversing their order still matter? Assume the query returns the same rows either way, but the data distributions are quite different.

Both (A, B) and (B, A) can form a precise seek when both receive equality conditions, so their lookup behavior for that query may be similar. Order still affects compression, tree shape, estimates, sorting support, and usefulness to other queries that constrain only one column. Include range predicates and ordering requirements in the decision; choosing solely by which equality column is more selective is often incomplete.
What must an index store for a query to avoid visiting the base table at all? Please distinguish key columns used for searching from additional columns carried only for output.

It must contain every value needed for predicates, joins, grouping, ordering, and the returned columns. Key columns determine the B-tree's search order; many systems also allow included columns at the leaves, which cover output without affecting that order. The optimizer can then use an index-only or covering scan, although some engines still consult table-side visibility metadata to verify that an entry is visible.
If the query selects id and total while filtering on customer_id, would an index keyed by customer_id with id and total included be sufficient even though total is not part of the search ordering?

Generally, yes. Customer_id provides the seek key, while the leaf entries carry id and total for projection. The engine can return those values without fetching each base row, subject to its visibility rules and index capabilities. If the query adds a predicate or sort on total, the included copy can sometimes be filtered directly, but it does not provide B-tree ordering by total.

I might be wrong, but I think a covering index contains every column needed by a query, permitting execution without extra row lookups in the base table...? Are visibility checks an exception to that description?

That is the usual definition and benefit. Coverage means all query-required values are available from the index, eliminating ordinary base-row fetches for missing columns. Visibility is an implementation caveat rather than a failure of coverage: for example, an MVCC engine may need table metadata unless a visibility map proves the page safe for index-only access. Other engines keep enough visibility information with the index entry itself.
What costs can make a covering index unattractive despite fewer lookups? I am considering leaf-page width, cache residency, update frequency, and overlap with a narrower existing index.

Included values widen leaf entries, increasing storage, cache consumption, write-ahead logging, and the number of pages a scan must read. Changes to included columns may also require index maintenance. A wide covering index can reduce fan-out or split more often, depending on the engine. Compare its measured read savings with update cost and redundancy; sometimes a narrow index plus a modest number of table lookups performs better overall.
How are a clustered table, a secondary index, and a covering index related? The terms seem to describe physical ordering, access paths, and query-specific contents rather than competing categories.

They describe different properties. A clustered organization determines how base rows are arranged or keyed, usually with only one clustering choice. A secondary index is another access structure whose entries point to base rows or clustered keys. Covering is query-relative: either kind of index covers a particular query if it supplies every required column. A secondary index can therefore be covering without defining the table's physical order.
Can an index remove sorting for one query but not another even when both select only columns stored in that index? I suspect coverage and useful ordering are separate conditions.

Exactly. Coverage answers whether the index has all required values; ordering answers whether its key sequence matches the requested ORDER BY after accounting for equality-constrained prefixes, direction, collation, and null placement. Included columns can provide values without contributing order. Thus an index may cover both queries yet avoid sorting only for the one whose requested order aligns with its key definition.

I might be wrong, but I think a covering index contains every row in physical table order, permitting execution without filtering or sorting for any query...? Is “covering” actually a property of the whole table?

Covering is a property relative to one query, not a promise about physical row order or every query. The index contains entries for applicable rows and enough columns to answer that particular query without fetching base rows. Predicates may still require filtering, and sorting disappears only when the index's key order matches the requested order. Another query needing different columns or ordering may not be covered at all.
Could you give one compact example where an index is covering but still needs a sort, and another where it provides ordering but still requires base-row lookups?

For SELECT email FROM users ORDER BY created_at, an index on (email, created_at) contains both values but orders primarily by email, so a sort may remain. For SELECT email, biography FROM users ORDER BY created_at, an index on (created_at, email) supplies the requested order but lacks biography, requiring base-row lookups. Exact plans can differ with predicates, statistics, and an optimizer's preference for scanning versus sorting.
